gimlet: The gimlet first turns up by name in 1928, described as gin, a spot of lime and soda, but its roots lie in British maritime lime rations. In 1867 Lauchlan Rose of Leith patented a way to preserve lime juice without alcohol, the same year a Merchant Shipping Act required lime juice aboard British merchant ships, and the story goes that naval officers took to mixing it with gin. The name may come from the small hand drill; a tale crediting navy surgeon Sir Thomas Gimlette goes unmentioned in his obituaries.
hemingway-daiquiri: Ernest Hemingway became a regular at Havana's El Floridita in the 1930s, when head bartender Constantino Ribalaigua Vert had made the bar famous for its daiquiris. Hemingway took his without sugar, and the version the bar built for him, sharpened with grapefruit and maraschino, came to be called the Papa Doble after his nickname. El Floridita still trades on the connection, with a bronze statue of the writer leaning on the end of the bar.
jack-rose: The Jack Rose appears in print by 1905, when the National Police Gazette credited a New Jersey bartender, Frank J. May, with creating it. Its name has drawn several theories: a Newark restaurateur named Joseph P. Rose, the pink Jacqueminot rose, or simply applejack plus the drink's rosy colour, the likeliest of them; the drink predates the career of the gambler Bald Jack Rose. Hemingway gave it literary fame in 1926, when Jake Barnes drinks one in a Paris hotel bar in The Sun Also Rises.
last-word: The Last Word was on the menu of the Detroit Athletic Club by 1916, its inventor unknown, and the vaudeville performer Frank Fogarty carried it to New York later that decade. It survived in print in Ted Saucier's 1951 book Bottoms Up but was otherwise forgotten until the early 2000s, when Seattle bartender Murray Stenson found the recipe and put it on the menu at the Zig Zag Café. From there it spread across the country and inspired a family of equal-parts cocktails, the Paper Plane among them.
lemon-drop: The Lemon Drop is usually credited to Norman Jay Hobday at Henry Africa's in San Francisco in the 1970s. His bar is often described as the first of the fern bars, singles bars filled with plants and Tiffany-style lamps, a model that spread across the country. Named after the hard lemon candy it imitates, the drink began as sweetened vodka and lemon served up, and it travelled with the vodka boom of the following decades.
margarita: Mexico's news agency Notimex and many experts have said Francisco 'Pancho' Morales has the strongest claim; he said he mixed the first margarita at Tommy's Place in Ciudad Juárez on 4 July 1942. Rival claims include Carlos 'Danny' Herrera's Rancho La Gloria in Baja California, a story since challenged, and the Dallas socialite Margarita Sames, who dated hers to 1948 in Acapulco, though Jose Cuervo was already advertising margaritas by 1945. Historian David Wondrich sees it as a tequila version of the daisy, and margarita is Spanish for daisy.
paper-plane: Sam Ross created the Paper Plane in 2008 for a menu at The Violet Hour in Chicago, naming it after M.I.A.'s song Paper Planes, which he was listening to often at the time. The first version used Campari, but Ross soon switched to Aperol for a lighter, rounder drink. Built in equal parts, a nod to the Last Word, it was passed from bartender to bartender and became one of the few drinks of its era already treated as a modern classic.
penicillin: Australian bartender Sam Ross created the Penicillin at Milk & Honey in New York in 2005, building a sour on blended Scotch with lemon and a honey-ginger syrup, then floating a smoky Islay malt on top. He originally made it with Compass Box whiskies for both the base and the float. It never needed an advertising campaign: bartenders who tasted it took it back to their own menus, and within a few years it was being served around the world.
pisco-sour: The pisco sour as it is known today was developed in Lima in the early 1920s at Morris' Bar, which American bartender Victor Vaughen Morris opened in 1916; the oldest known mention of the drink appeared in the magazine Hogar in 1920. Mario Bruiget, who began working for Morris in 1924, is credited with adding egg white and Angostura bitters. Chile's rival claim, crediting a steward named Elliot Stubb in Iquique, appears to rest on a source describing the whiskey sour, and Peru marks National Pisco Sour Day each February.
sidecar: The Sidecar's first printed recipes appeared in 1922, in Robert Vermeire's Cocktails and How to Mix Them and Harry MacElhone's Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails, which credited Pat MacGarry of Buck's Club in London. Paris has its own claims, from the Ritz to MacElhone's own Harry's New York Bar, and a popular story names an American army captain in wartime Paris who rode to his favourite bar in a motorcycle sidecar. The name is usually taken to come from that attachment, common at the time.
ward-8: The usual story says the Ward 8 was first mixed at Boston's Locke-Ober restaurant in 1898 to celebrate Martin Lomasney's election to the state legislature from the city's Eighth Ward, a political machine stronghold, with the toast raised the night before the votes were counted. Historians treat the tale with caution, but the name stuck to this rye sour with orange and grenadine, which appears in cocktail books from the early twentieth century onward.
whiskey-sour: Sours grew out of the punch tradition of mixing spirits with citrus and sugar. The oldest known mention of a whiskey sour by name is in an 1870 Wisconsin newspaper, though Jerry Thomas's 1862 bartender's guide had already printed sours made with brandy and gin. Shaken with egg white it is often called a Boston Sour, and with a float of dry red wine it becomes a New York Sour. The template of spirit, citrus and sugar went on to shape the daiquiri, the margarita and the sidecar.
aperol-spritz: The spritz began with Habsburg soldiers and officials in the nineteenth-century Veneto, who found the local wines strong and asked for them spritzed with water. Between the 1920s and 1930s Venetian bars began adding local bitter aperitifs, and Aperol, made in nearby Padua, became the basis of the most famous version; prosecco replaced still wine in the 1970s. The Aperol Spritz joined the International Bartenders Association's official list in 2011 and spread worldwide over the following decade.
bellini: Giuseppe Cipriani, who had founded Harry's Bar in Venice, gave the Bellini its name in 1948, mixing white peach purée with prosecco during the summer peach season. He named it after the fifteenth-century Venetian painter Giovanni Bellini, because its pink glow reminded him of the colour of a saint's robe in one of Bellini's paintings. The drink became the signature of Harry's Bar and travelled with the Cipriani name to restaurants around the world.
champagne-cocktail: The Champagne Cocktail was already a known American drink by 1862, when Jerry Thomas printed it in his pioneering bartender's guide, and it remained a staple of hotel bars through the Victorian era and beyond. Many later recipes added a splash of brandy or cognac to the original of sugar, bitters and wine. It also turns up in Casablanca, where Victor Laszlo orders champagne cocktails at Rick's café.
death-in-the-afternoon: Ernest Hemingway contributed Death in the Afternoon to So Red the Nose, or Breath in the Afternoon, a 1935 collection of cocktail recipes by well-known writers, and named it after his 1932 book about bullfighting. It is one of the few cocktails credited directly to a novelist, and it pairs two drinks closely associated with France. When absinthe returned to legal sale in the United States and much of Europe, bartenders revived it along with other absinthe classics.
french-75: The French 75 took its name from the French 75mm field gun of the First World War, and Harry MacElhone, who would soon take over Harry's New York Bar in Paris, recorded an early '75' in 1922, made with calvados, gin, grenadine and absinthe. The familiar mix of gin, lemon, sugar and champagne appeared in the 1927 book Here's How, and The Savoy Cocktail Book spread it under the French 75 name in 1930. New York's Stork Club later made it a fixture in America.
mimosa: The Mimosa is usually credited to Frank Meier, bartender at the Ritz in Paris, around 1925, a few years after London's Buck's Club introduced the similar Buck's Fizz in 1921. It is named after the mimosa plant, whose bright yellow blossoms the drink's colour resembles. Easy to make with any sparkling wine, it became a fixture of hotel and restaurant brunch menus in the United States in the second half of the twentieth century.
negroni-sbagliato: Sbagliato means mistaken, and the story told by Mirko Stocchetto, owner of Bar Basso in Milan, is that in 1972 he reached for a bottle of sparkling wine instead of gin while making a Negroni, and the customer liked the result. Bar Basso has served it ever since in its oversized goblets, and for decades it stayed a Milanese speciality. In 2022 an interview clip in which the actor Emma D'Arcy named it as their drink of choice went viral and made it a request in bars around the world.
seelbach: The Seelbach was presented in 1995 as a rediscovered house cocktail of Louisville's Seelbach Hotel, supposedly a pre-Prohibition recipe, and the story was repeated in cocktail books for two decades. In 2016 its real creator, Adam Seger, who had run the hotel's bar, admitted that he had invented both the drink and its vintage backstory. The recipe has stayed on menus anyway, now with its true history attached.
black-russian: Belgian bartender Gustave Tops created the Black Russian in 1949 at the Hotel Metropole in Brussels, mixing it for Perle Mesta, the American socialite then serving as ambassador to Luxembourg. The name is usually read as pairing vodka, long associated with Russia, with the darkness of the coffee liqueur. Adding cream produced its better-known offspring, the White Russian, which first appears in print in the 1960s.
boulevardier: The Boulevardier appears in Harry MacElhone's 1927 book Barflies and Cocktails, where he credits it to Erskine Gwynne, an American writer in Paris who published a monthly magazine for expatriates called The Boulevardier. MacElhone's Harry's New York Bar, a gathering place for Americans in the city, was its natural home. The drink was largely forgotten for decades and returned with the cocktail revival of the early twenty-first century, when bartenders went looking for whiskey cousins of the Negroni.
hanky-panky: Ada Coleman, known as Coley, was head bartender at the American Bar of London's Savoy Hotel from the early 1900s, one of very few women in such a role. She created the Hanky Panky for the actor-manager Sir Charles Hawtrey, a regular who asked for something with punch; after tasting it he is said to have declared it the real hanky-panky, and the name stuck. Her successor Harry Craddock included it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930.
manhattan: The Manhattan was being mixed in New York by the early 1880s, when it first appears in print, and early accounts tie it to the city's Manhattan Club. The popular story that it was created for a banquet thrown by Jennie Jerome, Winston Churchill's mother, falls apart because she was in England at the time, about to give birth to Winston. Rye was the original base, and the drink became the model for a whole family of whiskey and vermouth cocktails.
martinez: The Martinez first appears in print in 1884, in O.H. Byron's The Modern Bartender's Guide, and Jerry Thomas's 1887 guide gave it Old Tom gin, vermouth, maraschino and bitters. Its origin is disputed: one story credits Thomas at San Francisco's Occidental Hotel, mixing for a traveller bound for the town of Martinez, while Martinez itself says a local bartender invented it and marks the claim with a plaque. Either way, it is widely seen as a forerunner of the Martini.
martini: The Martini's origins are disputed, but it appears by that name in Harry Johnson's bartender's manual of 1888, made with Old Tom gin and vermouth and close kin to the Martinez. Some trace the name to the Martinez, others to the Martini brand of Italian vermouth. Dry versions followed early in the twentieth century, among the first printed by San Francisco bartender William Boothby, and the drink grew steadily drier, inspiring quips about vermouth, including one attributed to Churchill that is probably apocryphal.
negroni: The usual story says that around 1919, at the Caffè Casoni in Florence, Count Camillo Negroni asked bartender Fosco Scarselli to strengthen his Americano by replacing the soda water with gin, and Scarselli swapped the lemon garnish for orange to mark the difference. Historians still debate details of the account, including the count's title. The drink spread slowly beyond Italy and became one of the defining cocktails of the craft revival.
old-fashioned: The Old Fashioned descends from the original cocktail, defined in a Hudson, New York, newspaper in 1806 as spirits, sugar, water and bitters. As bartenders added liqueurs and absinthe to their whiskey cocktails later in the century, customers who wanted the plain version began asking for an old-fashioned one, and by the 1880s the name had stuck. Louisville's Pendennis Club claims to have popularised it, and in 2015 the city named it its official cocktail.
sazerac: The Sazerac takes its name from Sazerac de Forge et Fils, a cognac sold at New Orleans' Sazerac Coffee House, which opened in the 1850s, and the house cocktail was seasoned with the bitters created by Creole apothecary Antoine Peychaud. Rye whiskey later replaced the cognac, in part because phylloxera devastated French vineyards, and the absinthe rinse became part of the ritual. In 2008 the Louisiana legislature named it the official cocktail of New Orleans.
vesper: Ian Fleming invented the Vesper in Casino Royale, his first James Bond novel, published in 1953, in which Bond orders gin, vodka and Kina Lillet and names the drink after the double agent Vesper Lynd. Fleming is said to have based it on a drink made by his friend Ivar Bryce. The original Kina Lillet was reformulated in 1986 into the less bitter Lillet Blanc, so bartenders now reach for other quinquina aperitifs to approximate the drink Fleming described.
vieux-carre: Walter Bergeron, head bartender at the Hotel Monteleone in New Orleans, created the Vieux Carré in the 1930s, and it was recorded in Stanley Clisby Arthur's guide Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em. Vieux Carré, the old square, is the historic name for the French Quarter, where the hotel stands. The Monteleone's Carousel Bar, which still makes one slow turn every fifteen minutes, keeps the drink on its menu.
hugo-spritz: Roland Gruber, a bartender in Naturns in South Tyrol, created the Hugo in 2005 as an alternative to the Aperol Spritz, originally sweetening it with lemon balm syrup. Elderflower syrup soon took over because it was easier to find, and the drink spread through the Alpine resorts of northern Italy, Austria and Germany. Gruber has said he chose the name Hugo almost at random, and it became one of the most popular new spritzes in Europe.
kir-royale: The Kir Royale is the champagne version of the kir, the Burgundian aperitif of white wine and crème de cassis once known simply as blanc-cassis. The drink took the name of Canon Félix Kir, a priest and Resistance figure who served as mayor of Dijon from 1945 until 1968 and poured it at civic receptions to promote the region's wine and cassis. Swapping the still Aligoté for champagne turned a local habit into an international aperitif.
bahama-mama: The Bahama Mama has no fully documented origin, but Bahamian bartender Oswald 'Slade' Greenslade said he created it at the Nassau Beach Hotel in 1961 and named it in tribute to a local calypso singer. His version mixed aged and overproof rums with coffee liqueur, lemon and pineapple, while later chain-restaurant recipes dropped the coffee liqueur for coconut and banana. It belongs to the era of sweet, colourful rum house drinks made for visitors to Caribbean resorts.
blue-hawaii: Harry Yee, head bartender at what is now the Hilton Hawaiian Village in Waikiki, created the Blue Hawaii in 1957 after a sales representative from the Dutch liqueur maker Bols asked him to build a drink around blue curaçao. Yee, who is also credited with popularising paper umbrellas and orchids as tropical garnishes, built a pineapple sour around the liqueur. It shares its name with the Elvis Presley film shot in Hawaii, which came four years later.
fog-cutter: Victor 'Trader Vic' Bergeron published the Fog Cutter in his Bartender's Guide in the late 1940s, one of the house drinks of his Oakland restaurant, which had started life as a bar called Hinky Dinks. It became a fixture of mid-century tiki menus, served at his restaurants in its own tall ceramic mug, and it travelled with the Trader Vic's chain to cities around the world. Tiki historians have since kept his original recipe in circulation.
jungle-bird: Malaysian beverage manager Jeffrey Ong created the Jungle Bird in 1973 as a welcome drink at the Aviary Bar of the Kuala Lumpur Hilton, naming it after the tropical birds kept in the aviary visible from the bar. It first appeared in print in John J. Poister's 1989 New American Bartender's Guide. In 2010 New York bartender Giuseppe González reworked it with blackstrap rum and less pineapple, the version most bars now follow.
navy-grog: Donn Beach, founder of Don the Beachcomber in Hollywood, is generally credited with the Navy Grog in the 1940s, and Trader Vic later served his own version. The name recalls grog, the watered rum ration that Admiral Edward Vernon, nicknamed Old Grog for his grogram coat, ordered for his ships in 1740. Donn built his on several rums, and Richard Nixon was reportedly fond of the version served at Trader Vic's in Washington.
rum-runner: The Holiday Isle Tiki Bar in Islamorada, in the Florida Keys, claims the Rum Runner, usually dating it to the early 1970s. The bar's story is that its staff invented the drink to use up surplus banana and blackberry liqueurs before an inventory count. The name honours the smugglers who ran rum into the Keys from the Bahamas and Cuba during Prohibition, and the drink became the frozen signature of Keys beach bars.
saturn: The Saturn is credited to J. 'Popo' Galsini, a Filipino-American bartender in California, who won the International Bartenders Association's World Cocktail Championship with it in 1967. It stands out as a gin-based tiki drink, built on passion fruit, orgeat, falernum and lemon, and its garnish, a cherry ringed by lemon peel, is said to suggest the planet. Largely forgotten after the tiki era faded, it was brought back by bartenders and drink historians during the cocktail revival.
scorpion-bowl: Trader Vic said he based the Scorpion on a punch he encountered in Honolulu, and the recipe appeared in his Bartender's Guide in the late 1940s. Served in a wide ceramic bowl with long straws and a floating gardenia, it became one of the defining shared drinks of the tiki era, and Polynesian and Chinese-American restaurants across the United States kept it on their menus for decades after the tiki craze faded.
suffering-bastard: Joe Scialom, head bartender at Shepheard's Hotel in Cairo, created the Suffering Bastard in 1942, when the hotel was a gathering place for British officers during the North African campaign. He mixed gin and brandy with lime, bitters and ginger beer, and the blunt name is said to have come from his officer customers; one story has the hotel sending it to troops near El Alamein. Trader Vic later served a different rum drink under the same name, which spread it through American tiki bars.
three-dots-and-a-dash: Donn Beach created Three Dots and a Dash at Don the Beachcomber in Hollywood in the 1940s, during the Second World War, naming it after the Morse code for the letter V, the Allied signal for victory. Like many of Donn's recipes, it was guarded behind coded ingredient names so rivals could not copy it. Tiki historian Jeff 'Beachbum' Berry later published an accurate version, and it returned to tiki bars with the revival.
hurricane: Pat O'Brien's in New Orleans created the Hurricane in the 1940s, when wartime liquor distributors made bars buy cases of rum in order to get scarce whiskey. The bar needed a way to sell the surplus, so it mixed rum with passion fruit syrup and citrus and served it in tall glasses shaped like hurricane lamps, which gave the drink its name. It remains Pat O'Brien's signature and a fixture of the French Quarter.
mai-tai: Victor 'Trader Vic' Bergeron said he created the Mai Tai at his Oakland restaurant in 1944 for two friends visiting from Tahiti, one of whom tasted it and exclaimed 'maita'i roa ae', roughly 'out of this world', which gave it its name. Donn Beach disputed the claim, pointing to his earlier Q.B. Cooler, and the argument has never been fully settled. It became the emblem of the tiki age, and many later versions added the pineapple juice his original never had.
painkiller: The Painkiller comes from the Soggy Dollar Bar on Jost Van Dyke in the British Virgin Islands, where Daphne Henderson served it in the 1970s; the bar has no dock, so visitors swim ashore and pay with wet money, which gave the bar its name. In the 1980s Charles Tobias, founder of Pusser's Rum, popularised the drink and trademarked the name for versions made with Pusser's, which has kept it tied to his rum ever since.
pina-colada: The Caribe Hilton in San Juan credits its bartender Ramón 'Monchito' Marrero with creating the Piña Colada in 1954, blending rum with pineapple juice and Coco López, the cream of coconut developed on the island. A colleague at the hotel, Ricardo García, also claimed it, and the Barrachina restaurant in Old San Juan says its bartender Ramón Portas Mingot invented it in 1963. The name means strained pineapple, and Puerto Rico made the Piña Colada its official national drink in 1978.
sex-on-the-beach: Sex on the Beach belongs to the 1980s wave of peach schnapps drinks that followed the launch of DeKuyper's Peachtree, and its origin is loosely documented. One widely repeated story credits Ted Pizio, a bartender at Confetti's in Fort Lauderdale, who is said to have created it in 1987 for a schnapps sales contest. Recipes vary from bar to bar, but a version with cranberry juice now sits on the International Bartenders Association's official cocktail list.
singapore-sling: Ngiam Tong Boon, a Hainanese bartender at the Long Bar of Raffles Hotel in Singapore, is credited with creating the Singapore Sling around 1915. Slings, mixtures of spirit, sugar and water, were already an old American form, but his pink, fruit-laden version became the hotel's signature. The original recipe was lost and argued over for decades, and the version Raffles serves today is widely considered a later reconstruction; the Long Bar still lets guests drop peanut shells on the floor.
zombie: Donn Beach created the Zombie at Don the Beachcomber in Hollywood in 1934. He guarded the recipe closely, writing ingredients in code so that his bartenders mixed from unlabelled bottles, and the drink was widely imitated, often badly. In 2007 tiki historian Jeff 'Beachbum' Berry published what he identified as Donn's original recipe, decoded from a 1937 notebook kept by one of Donn's bartenders, and it has since returned to tiki menus.
bacanora: Bacanora takes its name from the town of Bacanora in the Sonoran sierra, where families have roasted and distilled local agave for generations. During the Mexican Revolution, Sonora's governor Plutarco Elías Calles banned alcohol production in the state, and bacanora went underground for most of the twentieth century until legal production returned in the early nineties. It later won its own denomination of origin, which limits the name to agave spirit made in designated Sonoran municipalities.
mezcal-anejo: Mezcal añejo exists as a class because of rules: when Mexico gave mezcal its denomination of origin in 1994, the official standard sorted it by age, and añejo meant spirit rested at least a year in wood. A 2016 revision kept the class while adding categories for how the mezcal is made: mezcal, artisanal mezcal and ancestral mezcal. Most producers still bottle young, so añejos remain a small corner of the category, made from whichever agave the maker chooses, since mezcal, unlike tequila, can use dozens of species.
mezcal-de-pechuga: Pechuga is a village tradition rather than an invention with a date. In parts of Oaxaca and neighbouring states, mezcaleros have long made a special batch for weddings, feasts and saints' days by redistilling finished mezcal with seasonal fruit, grains and spices. The name, Spanish for breast, refers to the chicken or turkey breast hung inside the still during that final pass. No one has recorded who first did it, and for most of its history pechuga was made for family and community celebrations rather than for sale.
mezcal-joven: Mezcal's name comes from the Nahuatl mexcalli, 'cooked agave', and people in Mexico were roasting and fermenting agave long before anyone distilled it. Distillation is usually dated to the 1500s, after the Spanish conquest, and one widely held view credits Filipino sailors on the Manila galleons with bringing the simple stills still used for ancestral mezcal. Joven, also called blanco, is the original unaged form, and Oaxaca, home to most production, remained its heartland when the denomination of origin was drawn in 1994.
mezcal-reposado: Reposado, 'rested', became a formal mezcal class in 1994, when Mexico's first official mezcal standard defined it as spirit aged in wood for two months to a year, a middle step between the young spirit most mezcaleros prefer and the rarer añejo. The class carried over into the 2016 revision of the standard. Like most mezcal, reposados are usually made from espadín, a cultivated agave favoured because it matures faster than wild species.
mezcal-tobala: Tobalá is the common name for Agave potatorum, a small, broad-leaved wild agave that grows in the rocky highlands of Oaxaca and Puebla, often in the shade of oak trees. It has no single creator or founding date; mezcaleros have long gathered it from the hills to distil in small batches. Because the plant reproduces only from seed rather than sending up clones, wild stands recover slowly, and some producers now raise tobalá from seed in nurseries to keep it from being overharvested.
raicilla: Raicilla comes from the mountains and coast of western Jalisco, where it has been distilled for around three centuries from several local agave species. Its name means 'little root', and the usual story is that producers chose it in colonial times so their agave spirit would escape the taxes and bans aimed at mezcal. For generations it was sold informally, until Mexico granted it a denomination of origin covering a group of municipalities in Jalisco and one in Nayarit.
sotol: Sotol is distilled from Dasylirion, the desert spoon, a plant of the Chihuahuan Desert that is not an agave at all. Indigenous peoples of the region, including the Rarámuri, were fermenting it into a beer-like drink centuries before distilled sotol appeared. Like other rural spirits it was long made outside the law, and Mexico has since granted it a denomination of origin for Chihuahua, Coahuila and Durango, and in Chihuahua it is the official state spirit. A plant can take around a decade to mature.
tequila-anejo: Tequila became Mexico's first denomination of origin in 1974, and the official standards that followed sorted it by age, reserving the word añejo, 'aged', for tequila matured in oak barrels of no more than 600 litres, so the wood keeps a close grip on the spirit. Many producers use former American whiskey casks, and some finish their añejos in cognac, sherry or wine barrels. For decades añejo was the top of the scale, until extra añejo was added above it.
tequila-blanco: Tequila takes its name from the town of Tequila in Jalisco, where by the mid-1700s the agave spirit distilled in the surrounding highland valleys had come to be called after the town. In 1795 the Spanish crown granted José María Guadalupe de Cuervo one of the first licences to make it commercially, and later Cenobio Sauza, credited with championing blue agave, became the first to export tequila to the United States. Blanco, bottled unaged or rested under two months, is the oldest style, and tequila became Mexico's first denomination of origin in 1974.
tequila-cristalino: Cristalino is a twenty-first-century idea: take añejo or extra añejo tequila and filter it through activated charcoal until the barrel colour is gone. The style is usually traced to Don Julio 70, launched in 2011 to mark seventy years since Don Julio González began making tequila in 1942, and widely marketed as the first clear añejo. Mexican rules do not treat cristalino as its own class, so bottles are labelled by their underlying age, and many large houses have followed with versions of their own.
tequila-extra-anejo: Extra añejo is the youngest official class of tequila, created in 2006 when Mexico revised its tequila standard to recognise spirit aged at least three years in oak. Producers had already been releasing very old tequilas as luxury bottlings, often in elaborate decanters, and the new class gave them a regulated name above añejo. The same 600-litre limit on barrel size applies as for añejo.
tequila-joven: Joven, also sold as oro or gold, is the class Mexican rules set aside for blends: blanco mixed with rested or aged tequila, or blanco softened with permitted additives such as caramel colour. The inexpensive gold tequilas familiar in American bars in the late twentieth century were mostly mixtos, which need only 51 percent agave sugars, and most owed their colour to caramel rather than time in a barrel. A few producers make joven by blending 100 percent agave blanco with older tequila.
tequila-reposado: Reposado means 'rested', and it is one of the age classes Mexico set out after tequila became the country's first denomination of origin in 1974. It has long been among the most popular styles in Mexico itself, valued for the way a short spell in wood softens the agave without hiding it. Much of the resting happens in used American bourbon barrels, because bourbon law demands new charred oak and leaves a steady supply of empty casks heading south.
aperol: Brothers Luigi and Silvio Barbieri of Padua launched Aperol in 1919 after seven years of experiments with bitter orange, gentian, rhubarb and cinchona. The name is generally linked to the French apéro, for an aperitif. Venetian bars were soon mixing it into the local spritz of wine and soda water, and after the Campari Group bought the brand in 2003 the Aperol Spritz spread far beyond the Veneto to become a summer fixture around the world.
campari: Gaspare Campari created his bitter red aperitif in 1860 and made Milan its home, opening a café in the city's Galleria Vittorio Emanuele. His son Davide built the brand into an export business, opening the company's first factory at Sesto San Giovanni, just outside the city, in 1904, and commissioning posters from leading artists of the day. The recipe remains secret, though one change is public: the red long came from carmine, a dye made from cochineal insects, until the company switched colourings in 2006.
cynar: Cynar was launched in 1952 by Angelo Dalle Molle, a Venetian businessman, who built an amaro around the artichoke. The name comes from Cynara scolymus, the artichoke's botanical name, and the artichoke is one of thirteen herbs and plants in the recipe. Italian television advertising in the following decades made it a household name, and the Campari Group has made and distributed it since 1995, which helped carry it into cocktail bars abroad.
fernet-branca: Bernardino Branca, a self-taught herbalist, began selling Fernet-Branca in Milan in 1845, and the firm he founded with his sons, Fratelli Branca, is still run by the family. Its eagle-over-globe logo was designed in 1893 by the illustrator Leopoldo Metlicovitz. Exports to Argentina began early in the twentieth century, and the company opened a distillery in Buenos Aires in 1925, where fernet mixed with cola, fernet con coca, became a national favourite.
american-single-malt: The modern American single malt category grew from West Coast craft distillers in the 1990s, including Clear Creek in Oregon and St George Spirits in California. Producers such as Westland in Seattle and Balcones in Texas followed, and in 2016 a group of distillers formed the American Single Malt Whiskey Commission to press for a legal definition. The Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau finalised one in December 2024: all malted barley, from one distillery, mashed, distilled and matured in the United States.
bottled-in-bond-bourbon: The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 answered a problem of adulterated whiskey: rectifiers were stretching straight whiskey with neutral spirit, colouring and flavouring, and honest distillers wanted a way to prove what was in the bottle. Colonel Edmund H. Taylor Jr. and Treasury Secretary John G. Carlisle championed the law, which put bonded warehouses under government seal so the government could vouch for what came out of them. It arrived nine years before the Pure Food and Drug Act, making it one of America's earliest consumer-protection laws.
bourbon: Corn-based whiskey was being distilled in Kentucky by the late 1700s, but bourbon has no single inventor, and the story crediting Baptist minister Elijah Craig with charring barrels is generally considered a legend. The name's origin is disputed: one theory points to Old Bourbon, the Virginia county created in 1785 whose name was marked on whiskey shipped downriver, while historian Michael Veach argues for Bourbon Street in New Orleans. In 1964 Congress declared bourbon a distinctive product of the United States.
cask-strength-bourbon: Every bourbon comes out of the barrel at cask strength; the style is simply the choice not to add water before bottling. Federal rules cap the proof at which bourbon may enter the barrel, but not the strength it reaches after years in a hot warehouse. The modern category is usually traced to Jim Beam master distiller Booker Noe, who bottled uncut, unfiltered bourbon as gifts for friends before Beam released it commercially as Booker's in 1988, and many distilleries now offer barrel-proof editions.
flavored-whiskey: Sweetened whiskey has American roots in rock and rye, a nineteenth-century bar staple of rye whiskey mellowed with rock candy and sometimes fruit. The modern flavoured category took off from the late 2000s, when large producers began adding honey, cinnamon, apple and other flavours, and Jack Daniel's Tennessee Honey, launched in 2011, became one of the most familiar examples. US rules let flavoured whisky be bottled at a lower strength than whisky itself, and the flavour must be named on the label.
high-rye-bourbon: High-rye has no legal definition; it describes bourbons whose recipes push rye well above the usual share while keeping the corn majority the law requires. The style is often associated with Old Grand-Dad, a brand Raymond B. Hayden named in honour of his grandfather Basil Hayden Sr., a Kentucky distiller remembered for using plenty of rye. Its well-known descendants include Basil Hayden's, and one of Four Roses' two mash bills contains 35 percent rye, among the highest of any major bourbon.
moonshine: Moonshine became an American tradition after 1791, when the new federal government taxed whiskey and backcountry farmers, many of them Scots-Irish settlers, kept distilling out of sight; resistance to the tax grew into the Whiskey Rebellion. The word was already English slang for smuggled spirits, a nod to work done by moonlight. Appalachia's hollows, with their poor roads and scattered farms, became the heartland of the trade through Prohibition, and licensed distillers have since revived the name for legal unaged corn whiskey.
rye-whiskey: Rye was the grain that grew most reliably for the German and Scots-Irish farmers of Pennsylvania and Maryland, and through the 1700s they distilled it into whiskey. Western Pennsylvania's Monongahela Valley became so identified with the style that Monongahela served as a name for rye itself, and resistance there to the 1791 federal whiskey tax grew into the Whiskey Rebellion. George Washington's Mount Vernon distillery made a rye-heavy whiskey in the late 1790s. Prohibition nearly wiped the category out, and its revival came with the cocktail boom.
single-barrel-bourbon: Single-barrel bottling as a marketed bourbon style began in 1984, when master distiller Elmer T. Lee created Blanton's at the George T. Stagg distillery in Frankfort, Kentucky, now Buffalo Trace. He named it for Colonel Albert B. Blanton, the distillery's longtime president, who was said to set aside barrels from the centre of its Warehouse H for himself. The stoppers show a horse and jockey in eight poses that together spell out the name, and many distilleries followed with single-barrel lines of their own.
small-batch-bourbon: Jim Beam credits its master distiller Booker Noe with bringing the phrase small batch into bourbon's vocabulary in 1988, when his uncut Booker's was drawn from a limited selection of barrels. In 1992 Beam built a range around the idea, the Small Batch Bourbon Collection of Booker's, Baker's, Basil Hayden's and Knob Creek. The term has no legal definition in the United States, so a batch can be any number of barrels a producer chooses, and it now appears on bottles from distilleries of every size.
straight-corn-whiskey: Corn whiskey is about as old as American distilling: settlers moving into Kentucky, Tennessee and the Virginia backcountry in the late 1700s grew corn and distilled much of it, usually selling the spirit young. Federal standards later set it apart from bourbon by requiring at least 80 percent corn and barring new charred oak, so aged corn whiskey rests in used or uncharred barrels. The straight label adds a minimum of two years in wood, a style kept alive by bottlings such as Heaven Hill's Mellow Corn.
tennessee-whiskey: Filtering new whiskey through sugar maple charcoal is an old Tennessee practice; for years a distiller named Alfred Eaton was said to have introduced it in 1825, though that claim has been disputed. It became known as the Lincoln County Process after the county where Jack Daniel's distillery first stood, before boundary changes moved the site into Moore County. Jack Daniel's, which now credits Nathan 'Nearest' Green, an enslaved man, with teaching young Jack to distil, made the style famous, and a 2013 state law requires the process, exempting only Benjamin Prichard's.
wheat-whiskey: Wheat has long been a flavouring grain in American whiskey, but a whiskey made mostly from wheat was a rarity until Heaven Hill released Bernheim Original Straight Wheat Whiskey in 2005, named after its Bernheim distillery in Louisville. US rules require at least 51 percent wheat in the mash, which separates it from wheated bourbon, whose mash is still mostly corn. Since then a handful of craft and large distillers have added wheat whiskeys, though the style remains a small corner of the market.
wheated-bourbon: Using wheat instead of rye as bourbon's flavouring grain is most closely tied to the Stitzel-Weller distillery, which Julian 'Pappy' Van Winkle opened in Louisville in 1935 to make bourbons such as W.L. Weller and Old Fitzgerald. In the 1950s Bill Samuels Sr. chose a wheated recipe for Maker's Mark, reportedly after baking loaves of bread from different grain mixes to compare them. Decades later the Van Winkle family's Pappy Van Winkle bottlings became so hard to find that wheated bourbon turned into a collectors' style.
absinthe: Absinthe began in the Val-de-Travers, in Switzerland's Neuchâtel region, in the late 1700s; legend credits a French doctor, Pierre Ordinaire, with a wormwood elixir around 1792, and the Henriod sisters of Couvet sold it as a remedy. In 1797 Major Dubied bought a recipe and opened a distillery in Couvet with his son-in-law Henri-Louis Pernod, who opened another at Pontarlier in France in 1805. Switzerland, the United States and France banned it in the 1910s, and the bans were lifted only decades later, in the United States in 2007.
arak: Arak belongs to the Levant's long distilling tradition, and its name comes from the Arabic 'araq, sweat, a nod to the drops that run from the still. In Lebanon it is made from local grapes such as obeideh and merwah, distilled with green aniseed and rested in clay jars, with the Bekaa Valley and the town of Zahlé as its most famous homes. Families and village distillers made it for generations, and no one is credited with inventing it; Lebanese wineries such as Ksara and Kefraya now make it too.
ouzo: Ouzo grew from tsipouro, the grape-pomace spirit long distilled by Greek monks and villagers, flavoured with anise. The first commercial ouzo distillery is usually dated to 1856, when Nikolaos Katsaros opened one in Tyrnavos in Thessaly. The name is disputed: one popular story links it to 'uso Marsiglia', stamped on Tyrnavos silk cocoons bound for Marseille, while Greek dictionaries prefer a Turkish root. Plomari on Lesbos became another famous centre, and in 2006 the EU reserved the name for Greece and Cyprus.
pastis: Paul Ricard, the son of a Marseille wine merchant, launched his pastis in 1932, in the years when France was cautiously allowing anise drinks back after banning absinthe during the First World War. He sold it as 'le vrai pastis de Marseille', and it became the emblem of the city's café terraces. The name comes from the Provençal pastis, a mix or muddle, and the style differs from absinthe by leaning on star anise and liquorice rather than wormwood.
raki: Rakı's exact beginnings are unknown, but grape-based anise spirits were distilled in the Ottoman Empire for centuries, and the traveller Evliya Çelebi wrote about rakı in the seventeenth century. Its name is generally traced to the Arabic 'araq. For a long time it was mostly made at home or by small producers, until the state monopoly Tekel took up industrial production in İzmir in the mid-twentieth century, and Turkey has since registered rakı as a geographical indication built on suma, the grape distillate, redistilled with aniseed in copper stills.
sambuca: Sambuca is usually traced to Civitavecchia, the port north of Rome, where Luigi Manzi sold an anise liqueur under the name around 1850. The name is commonly linked to sambucus, Latin for elder, though the plant's role in the recipe is debated. Another Civitavecchia native, Angelo Molinari, launched Molinari Sambuca Extra in 1945 and turned it into a national brand. Coffee beans floated on top are called la mosca, the fly, and a serving of three is said to stand for health, happiness and prosperity.
american-brandy: California's grape brandy goes back to the Spanish missions, whose friars planted the Mission grape and are said to have distilled some of their wine. After Prohibition the state's large wineries built big brandy brands, among them the De La Salle Christian Brothers, a Catholic teaching order whose Napa winery sold brandy under the order's name and used the proceeds to support its schools. A craft revival followed as small producers began working with alembic pot stills on the cognac model.
applejack: Apple brandy was a staple of colonial New Jersey, and the Laird family of Monmouth County traces its distilling to William Laird, a Scot said to have settled there in 1698. Laird & Company dates itself to 1780 and calls itself the oldest licensed distillery in the United States; George Washington reportedly asked the family for its recipe for cider spirits. The name applejack is often linked to 'jacking', the old practice of freezing cider and removing the ice, and the drink was nicknamed Jersey lightning.
armagnac: Armagnac has the oldest paper trail of any French brandy: around 1310, Vital du Four, a Gascon prior and later cardinal, praised the virtues of 'burning water', though historians debate whether he meant a local spirit. By the fifteenth century brandy was traded in Gascon markets, and Dutch merchants, eager for spirit that survived long voyages, later became important buyers. Its three districts, Bas-Armagnac, Ténarèze and Haut-Armagnac, were drawn by decree in the early twentieth century, and many producers remain small family estates.
brandy-de-jerez: Distilling around Jerez goes back to the Moors, who made wine spirit for perfume and medicine, and by the 1580s it was a large enough business for the town to tax it. Much of the low-strength spirit went to Holland, which is why it is still called holanda. The story goes that forgotten casks of it, left to age in sherry butts, showed what the solera could do, and Pedro Domecq's Fundador, launched in 1874, is often described as the first brandy de Jerez sold under a brand name.
calvados: The earliest record of cider distilling in Normandy comes from the diary of Gilles de Gouberville, a Cotentin squire, who noted it in 1553. The spirit takes its name from the Calvados département, created after the Revolution, whose own name is often said to come from a Spanish Armada ship, El Salvador, wrecked off the coast, though the story is uncertain. Calvados gained its protected appellation in 1942, with the double-distilled Pays d'Auge as the most exacting zone, and pears play a larger part in the Domfrontais.
cognac-vs: Cognac grew out of the Dutch and English trade along the Charente, where merchants found that distilled wine travelled better than wine itself, and double distillation became the local method in the seventeenth century. The English initials on its labels reflect that trade; VS stands for Very Special. In 1865 Maurice Hennessy introduced a star system for grading cognac, and three-star cognac, the house blend most producers sold, is the grade now labelled VS.
cognac-vsop: The VSOP grade, for Very Superior Old Pale, is usually traced to 1817, when the Prince Regent, the future King George IV, asked Hennessy for a cognac of that description. Pale is generally taken to mean a cognac without added colouring or sweetening, a selling point at the time. The term spread through the trade, and cognac's governing body later fixed it as a regulated age grade, sitting between the everyday VS and the long-aged XO.
cognac-xo: XO, for Extra Old, was introduced in 1870 by Maurice Hennessy, who blended older eaux-de-vie as a cognac for family and friends before it reached the market. Other houses adopted the name, and it became an official grade for blends whose youngest component had aged at least six years. In April 2018 cognac's rules raised that minimum to ten years, a change first planned for 2016 but postponed while producers built up older stocks.
french-brandy: Brandy itself is a Dutch-made word, from brandewijn, burnt wine, coined by the merchants who bought distilled French wine for shipping. French brandy as a separate category is a product of the law: in 1909 decrees drew the boundaries of Cognac and Armagnac, and grape spirit distilled anywhere else in France could only be sold as brandy, or under regional names such as Fine de Bourgogne. Labels such as St-Rémy have since carried it around the world.
grappa: Italian farmers distilled grape pomace long before anyone recorded when, using what was left after pressing the wine. The oldest working grappa distillery, Nardini, was founded in 1779 at Bassano del Grappa in the Veneto, and the town's name is often linked to the spirit's, though the word may instead come from grappolo, a bunch of grapes. In 1973 the Nonino family of Friuli distilled the first single-variety grappa, from Picolit pomace, helping turn a rough farm spirit into a refined digestivo.
kirschwasser: Kirschwasser, 'cherry water', comes from the orchards of the Black Forest and the Upper Rhine, where farmers have distilled small, dark, slightly bitter cherries for centuries; no one is credited with inventing it. Schwarzwälder Kirschwasser is now a protected geographical indication, and the spirit is so bound up with the region that German food guidelines require a cake sold as Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte, Black Forest cake, to contain it. Small farm distilleries across the region still make it.
palinka: Pálinka grew out of Hungary's village distilling, with families and local distilleries turning surplus orchard fruit into spirit for centuries. The word is generally traced to a Slavic root meaning to burn, as in the Slovak pálenka. Hungarian and EU law now protect the name: genuine pálinka must be distilled in Hungary from fruit grown there, with a lone exception for apricot spirit from four Austrian provinces, which may also use it.
